title: 'Protein Three-Dimensional Structure: The Sequence Sets the Shape'

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: The primary structure of a protein is its {{c1::amino acid sequence}}, written from the N-terminus to the C-terminus.
cards.back: Amino acids linked by peptide bonds into a chain, in one exact order.
cards.quote: The primary structure of a protein is its amino acid sequence: amino acids linked by peptide bonds into a chain
cards.section: One sequence, one shape

cards.front: State the chain of cause that links a protein's sequence to its job, and how sickle cell anemia shows it.
cards.back: Sequence dictates structure; structure dictates function; one changed residue can break both. In sickle cell, glutamate to valine at position 6 of beta-globin makes hemoglobin stick into fibers.
cards.quote: Sequence dictates structure. Structure dictates function. One changed residue can break both.
cards.section: One sequence, one shape

cards.front: For water-soluble proteins, what does the rule "geometry allows; water chooses" mean?
cards.back: The backbone can bend only a few ways, so only helices, strands and turns are possible. Among ways to pack them, the winner buries the oily side chains away from water and packs them well.
cards.quote: Among the ways to pack those pieces, the winner tucks the oily side chains inside, away from water, and packs them well.
cards.section: One sequence, one shape

cards.front: Ribonuclease is fully unfolded with urea and a reducing agent (zero activity). The chemicals are washed away, with no other proteins present and air available. Full activity returns. What does this show?
cards.back: The information for the fold is in the amino acid sequence itself, in a given environment. For most small proteins the fold is the lowest free-energy state the sequence can reach.
cards.why: Nothing else was in the tube, so no cellular machinery could have supplied the shape.
cards.quote: With nothing else in the tube, the information had to come from the chain itself.
cards.section: The proof: Anfinsen's refolding experiment

cards.front: Ribonuclease has eight cysteines that form four disulfide bonds. How many ways can eight cysteines pair, and how often would random pairing give the native set?
cards.back: First cysteine has 7 partners, next unpaired one 5, then 3, then 1: 7 × 5 × 3 × 1 = 105 pairings. Random chance of the native set is 1/105, about 0.95%, under 1%.
cards.quote: eight cysteines can pair in 7 × 5 × 3 × 1 = 105 different ways
cards.section: The proof: Anfinsen's refolding experiment

cards.front: Why are disulfide bonds found mostly in extracellular, secreted proteins?
cards.back: A disulfide forms only when two cysteine thiols are oxidized. The cytosol is reducing and keeps thiols free; the ER lumen and the outside of the cell are oxidizing, and secreted proteins make their disulfides in the ER.
cards.quote: Secreted proteins make their disulfides in the ER, which is why disulfides are found mostly in extracellular, secreted proteins.
cards.section: The proof: Anfinsen's refolding experiment

cards.front: Anfinsen's ribonuclease refolding is repeated, but the urea is removed while the reducing agent is kept in, so the solution stays reducing. Predict whether the native disulfides return, and why.
cards.back: They should not re-form. Disulfides form only when cysteine thiols are oxidized, and the original tube, open to air, was oxidizing.
cards.why: Rests on the rule that the fold is set by the sequence in a given environment, and on the oxidizing condition disulfides need.
cards.quote: Anfinsen's tube, open to air, was oxidizing too.
cards.section: The proof: Anfinsen's refolding experiment

cards.front: Why does the peptide bond not rotate?
cards.back: Resonance between two drawings gives the C–N bond partial double-bond character (short, about 1.32 Å). A double bond cannot twist without breaking its overlap, so six atoms are locked in one plane.
cards.quote: A double bond cannot twist without breaking its overlap, so the peptide bond does not rotate.
cards.section: The flat peptide bond: two hinges per residue

cards.front: Almost always the two Cα atoms sit on opposite sides of the peptide bond, the {{c1::trans}} form.
cards.back: The cis form is rare, though markedly more common in an X-Pro bond.
cards.quote: Almost always the two Cα atoms sit on opposite sides of the bond, the trans form.
cards.section: The flat peptide bond: two hinges per residue

cards.front: Which two backbone bonds per residue can rotate, and what are their angles called?
cards.back: Phi (φ), rotation about the N–Cα bond, and psi (ψ), rotation about the Cα–C bond. The third backbone bond, the peptide bond, is frozen.
cards.quote: phi (φ), the rotation about the N–Cα bond; psi (ψ), the rotation about the Cα–C bond.
cards.section: The flat peptide bond: two hinges per residue

cards.front: What does a Ramachandran plot show, and why is most of it forbidden?
cards.back: It plots φ against ψ (each −180° to +180°) and marks the pairs that do not clash. At most settings, atoms on neighbouring peptide planes would occupy the same space, so they are sterically disfavored.
cards.quote: Only a small fraction of φ/ψ space is accessible.
cards.section: The map of allowed shapes: the Ramachandran plot

cards.front: Name the three allowed regions of the Ramachandran plot and where each sits.
cards.back: Broad extended region for beta strands (upper left); compact right-handed alpha helix region near φ ≈ −57°, ψ ≈ −47° (lower left); small left-handed region (upper right), used mostly by glycine.
cards.quote: a compact region for the right-handed alpha helix, around φ ≈ −57°, ψ ≈ −47° (lower left)
cards.section: The map of allowed shapes: the Ramachandran plot

cards.front: Why does glycine reach more of the Ramachandran plot than any other residue?
cards.back: Its side chain is a single hydrogen. Every other residue has a Cβ that can bump into the backbone; glycine has none.
cards.quote: Every other residue has a Cβ, the first carbon of its side chain, which can bump into the backbone; glycine has none.
cards.section: The map of allowed shapes: the Ramachandran plot

cards.front: A new protein structure passes a Ramachandran check except for one active-site residue in a normally disfavored region. Is the structure wrong?
cards.back: Not necessarily. "Forbidden" means strongly disfavored, not impossible; a residue held by its surroundings can sit in a strained spot, and such outliers often matter for catalysis.
cards.why: Many residues in the forbidden zone would suggest an error; a single functional outlier does not.
cards.quote: A few residues, held by their surroundings, do sit in strained spots, and these outliers are often the ones that matter for catalysis.
cards.section: The map of allowed shapes: the Ramachandran plot

cards.front: Secondary structure is local shape built from hydrogen bonds between backbone {{c1::C=O and N–H}} groups.
cards.back: Helices and sheets; it describes a stretch of chain, not the whole protein.
cards.quote: Shapes built this way, from hydrogen bonds between backbone C=O and N–H groups, are secondary structure.
cards.section: Helices and sheets: the backbone bonds to itself

cards.front: In the interior of an alpha helix, which backbone groups are hydrogen-bonded?
cards.back: The C=O of residue i bonds to the N–H of residue i+4. The helix is right-handed with 3.6 residues per turn; side chains point outward.
cards.quote: every backbone C=O is hydrogen-bonded to the N–H four residues ahead (residue i to residue i+4)
cards.section: Helices and sheets: the backbone bonds to itself

cards.front: In a beta sheet, what is hydrogen-bonded to what, and how far apart in sequence can the partners be?
cards.back: Each nearly flat strand bonds to its neighbouring strands, parallel or antiparallel. The strands can lie far apart in sequence, unlike helix partners.
cards.quote: Each strand is hydrogen-bonded to its neighbouring strands, running parallel or antiparallel.
cards.section: Helices and sheets: the backbone bonds to itself

cards.front: A proline is introduced into an alpha helix. Where can it sit without breaking the helix, and why does it break the helix elsewhere?
cards.back: In the first turn, whose N–H groups have no partners four residues back anyway. In the middle it has no N–H to donate to the C=O four back, and its ring bumps the previous turn's backbone.
cards.quote: In the middle of a helix, proline breaks it for two reasons.
cards.section: Helices and sheets: the backbone bonds to itself

cards.front: Why must glycine occupy every third position of collagen's Gly-X-Y repeat?
cards.back: Three chains wind into a triple helix, and every third residue sits at its crowded center. Glycine is the only residue small enough to fit there.
cards.quote: Glycine, the only residue small enough, sits at the crowded center every third position.
cards.section: Helices and sheets: the backbone bonds to itself

cards.front: A mutation in type I collagen replaces a central-position glycine with a larger residue. Predict the effect on the triple helix and the disease that can result.
cards.back: The bulkier side chain cannot fit at the crowded center, so the triple helix is destabilized. This is one of the most common causes of osteogenesis imperfecta, brittle-bone disease.
cards.quote: Substitute a larger residue for glycine at that center of type I collagen and you get one of the most common causes of osteogenesis imperfecta, brittle-bone disease.
cards.section: Helices and sheets: the backbone bonds to itself

cards.front: Proline breaks alpha helices, yet collagen is rich in proline. Reconcile the two.
cards.back: The same rigid ring has opposite effects. In the middle of an alpha helix it lacks an N–H donor for the C=O four residues back and its ring bumps the prior turn; in collagen it pre-shapes each strand into the extended helix the triple helix needs.
cards.why: Rests on two stated rules: the helix needs i to i+4 backbone hydrogen bonds, and collagen strands are extended helices.
cards.quote: Collagen: the same ring, the opposite effect.
cards.section: Helices and sheets: the backbone bonds to itself

cards.front: What drives oily side chains together in water (the hydrophobic effect)?
cards.back: Water forms an ordered cage around oily surface, which is lost entropy. Bringing oily groups together exposes less surface, freeing caged water, and that entropy gain drives them together.
cards.quote: The freed water molecules tumble away and gain entropy. That gain is what drives the oily groups together.
cards.section: The hydrophobic core: water pushes oil inward

cards.front: A student says oily side chains cluster because oil attracts oil. What is wrong with this?
cards.back: Oily groups attract water about as well as each other, so that attraction gives no net preference. They are pushed together by water, not pulled together by each other.
cards.quote: Oily groups do attract each other, but they attract water about as well, so that attraction gives them no net preference.
cards.section: The hydrophobic core: water pushes oil inward

cards.front: The hydrophobic effect is the main driving force of {{c1::tertiary}} structure.
cards.back: Tertiary structure: the whole chain packed into a compact 3D shape by side chains far apart in sequence.
cards.quote: The hydrophobic effect is the main driving force of tertiary structure, the whole chain packed into a compact 3D shape by interactions between side chains far apart in sequence.
cards.section: The hydrophobic core: water pushes oil inward

cards.front: Why does burying part of the backbone in the core favor helices and sheets?
cards.back: Buried backbone C=O and N–H groups lose their water partners, and a buried polar group with no partner costs free energy. Hydrogen-bonding to itself in helices and sheets is the cheapest fix.
cards.quote: A buried polar group with no partner costs free energy.
cards.section: The hydrophobic core: water pushes oil inward

cards.front: A water-soluble protein contains leucine, valine, lysine and aspartate. Predict where each side chain mostly sits in the folded protein.
cards.back: Leucine and valine (nonpolar) are buried in the core; lysine and aspartate (charged) sit on the surface, hydrogen-bonding with water.
cards.quote: So in a water-soluble protein, nonpolar side chains are buried in a core and polar and charged side chains sit on the surface
cards.section: The hydrophobic core: water pushes oil inward

cards.front: What is quaternary structure, and what holds it together?
cards.back: Several folded chains held together as one unit, by the same non-covalent forces as tertiary structure (burial of nonpolar surface, hydrogen bonds, salt bridges), now acting between chains.
cards.quote: It uses the same non-covalent forces as tertiary structure, now acting between chains.
cards.section: Between chains: quaternary structure

cards.front: Myoglobin is a single chain folded around a heme; hemoglobin is four myoglobin-like chains. What is the highest level of structure each has?
cards.back: Myoglobin: tertiary, with no quaternary structure. Hemoglobin: quaternary, two alpha and two beta subunits working as one.
cards.quote: Hemoglobin is two alpha and two beta subunits, each myoglobin-like, working as one.
cards.section: Between chains: quaternary structure

cards.front: How does the glutamate-to-valine change at position 6 of beta-globin make sickle hemoglobin form fibers?
cards.back: It puts a nonpolar residue on the surface, a sticky patch. Releasing oxygen exposes an oily pocket, and the patch on one hemoglobin fits the pocket on a neighbour, so molecules stack into fibers.
cards.quote: The patch on one hemoglobin fits into that pocket on a neighbouring one, and the molecules stack into long fibers.
cards.section: Between chains: quaternary structure

cards.front: Sickle hemoglobin is kept fully oxygenated. Predict whether fibers form, and why.
cards.back: Fiber formation should be suppressed. The valine patch needs the oily pocket on a neighbour, and that pocket is exposed only when hemoglobin releases oxygen and changes shape.
cards.why: Rests on the stated mechanism: surface patch plus oxygen-release pocket builds an interface that should not exist.
cards.quote: Releasing oxygen changes hemoglobin's shape and exposes an oily pocket.
cards.section: Between chains: quaternary structure

cards.front: The melting temperature (Tm) is the temperature at which {{c1::half the molecules are unfolded}}.
cards.quote: The melting temperature (Tm) is the temperature at which half the molecules are unfolded.
cards.section: Only just stable: the melt

cards.front: {{c1::Cooperativity}} means a protein's structure unfolds as one unit.
cards.back: Contacts support each other like a house of cards; a small single-domain protein often melts over roughly ten degrees, a steep curve.
cards.quote: Cooperativity means the structure unfolds as one unit
cards.section: Only just stable: the melt

cards.front: Why can heat, or one bad residue, unfold a folded protein?
cards.back: Favorable contacts and freed water only just pay for the chain's lost freedom, so the folded protein is only marginally more stable than the coil. A small cost can erase the margin.
cards.quote: The favorable contacts and freed water only just pay for the chain's lost freedom, so a folded protein is only marginally more stable than the coil.
cards.section: Only just stable: the melt

cards.front: Two point mutants of a small water-soluble protein: a buried leucine becomes lysine; a surface aspartate becomes glutamate. Which lowers Tm, and why?
cards.back: The buried leucine to lysine. A charged residue in the core has no water to hydrogen-bond with and breaks the oily packing. The surface swap keeps the same charge, still in water, so Tm barely changes.
cards.quote: Buried in the core, it has no water to hydrogen-bond with, and it breaks up the oily packing.
cards.section: Only just stable: the melt

cards.front: An enzyme has Tm 62 °C; a core mutant has Tm 36 °C (made-up data). Both are assayed at 37 °C. Predict the mutant's activity and explain.
cards.back: Reduced. At 37 °C the mutant is above its Tm, so more than half its molecules are unfolded and inactive; the wild type, well below its Tm, is mostly folded.
cards.why: Combines the definition of Tm with sequence-structure-function: an unfolded enzyme cannot work.
cards.quote: That is why heat can undo it, and why one bad residue can tip it.
cards.section: Only just stable: the melt

cards.front: A 100-residue chain gets three backbone shapes per residue and tries one shape every 10⁻¹³ s. How many shapes, and how long to try them all?
cards.back: 3¹⁰⁰ ≈ 5 × 10⁴⁷ shapes. 5 × 10⁴⁷ × 10⁻¹³ s ≈ 5 × 10³⁴ s ≈ 10²⁷ years, versus a universe about 10¹⁰ years old. Small proteins fold in microseconds to seconds: Levinthal's paradox.
cards.quote: Suppose it could try a new shape every 10⁻¹³ seconds, about as fast as a bond can turn.
cards.section: Finding the fold fast: Levinthal's paradox and the funnel

cards.front: Someone argues the Ramachandran plot solves Levinthal's paradox. Test it: allow only two shapes per residue in a 100-residue chain, at one shape per 10⁻¹³ s.
cards.back: 2¹⁰⁰ ≈ 10³⁰ shapes; × 10⁻¹³ s ≈ 10¹⁷ s, about 4 billion years. Still far too slow, so fewer shapes per residue is not the answer.
cards.why: A per-residue filter shrinks each factor but leaves a hundred factors; the search is fast because it is biased.
cards.quote: A filter that works one residue at a time makes each factor smaller, but there are still a hundred factors.
cards.section: Finding the fold fast: Levinthal's paradox and the funnel

cards.front: According to the folding funnel, why does a chain find its fold fast?
cards.back: Native-like contacts each lower the energy a little, so the landscape slopes toward the fold. Once the first few contacts are in place, a small preference at each step is enough, since correct contacts tend to last and wrong ones break apart; for small proteins the first steps are slightly uphill.
cards.quote: The interactions that make the fold stable also guide the chain to it.
cards.section: Finding the fold fast: Levinthal's paradox and the funnel

cards.front: Many core nonpolar residues of a small protein are replaced with polar ones. Beyond lower stability, predict the effect on how readily it finds its fold.
cards.back: Folding should be slower or less reliable, an inference from the lesson's rule. The forces that slope the funnel are the same ones that stabilize the fold, so weakening core contacts should flatten the slope.
cards.why: Rests on the funnel rule: native-like contacts that free ordered water are what tilt the landscape.
cards.quote: What makes the slope? The same forces that make the fold stable.
cards.section: Finding the fold fast: Levinthal's paradox and the funnel

cards.front: Cells make chaperones. Does that contradict Anfinsen's conclusion that the sequence sets the fold?
cards.back: No. Real funnels have kinetic traps; chaperones stop half-folded chains from clumping and raise the yield, but they do not choose the destination. The sequence, in its environment, still does.
cards.quote: They do not choose the destination. The sequence, in its environment, still does.
cards.section: Finding the fold fast: Levinthal's paradox and the funnel

cards.front: A protein sequence has very few nonpolar residues and a large net charge. Predict its structure on its own in water.
cards.back: Likely intrinsically disordered, with no stable fold, because it cannot pay for a hydrophobic core. Many such proteins fold only when they meet a partner.
cards.quote: Their sequences have too few nonpolar residues and too much net charge to pay for a core.
cards.section: Where the rule bends

cards.front: How do prions bend the rule that one sequence sets one shape?
cards.back: The same sequence reaches a second stable fold, rich in beta sheet, that aggregates and kills; the normal prion protein is helix-rich. A sequence sets a shape, or a set of shapes, for a given environment.
cards.quote: Prions take the same sequence to a second stable fold, rich in beta sheet, that aggregates and kills.
cards.section: Where the rule bends

cards.front: What is unusual about the working fold of serpins such as alpha-1-antitrypsin?
cards.back: It is not their most stable fold. The working fold is a kinetic trap; the lowest free-energy state is a more stable, inactive form.
cards.quote: The working fold is a kinetic trap; the lowest free-energy state is a more stable, inactive form.
cards.section: Where the rule bends

cards.front: A protein segment spans a lipid membrane. Predict which kind of side chains face outward toward the lipid, and why.
cards.back: Greasy, nonpolar side chains. The solvent is lipid, not water, so the rule flips and so does the surface.
cards.quote: Membrane proteins sit in lipid, not water, so the solvent is flipped and so is their surface: greasy residues face the lipid.
cards.section: Where the rule bends

cards.front: Estimate the mass of myoglobin, a single chain of 153 residues, using the average residue mass.
cards.back: 153 × 110 Da ≈ 16,830 Da, about 17 kDa (within the usual 5 to 200 kDa range).
cards.quote: Multiply residues by 110 for daltons and divide by 1,000 for kilodaltons; most proteins are 5 to 200 kDa.
cards.section: A rule of thumb: protein mass
